title: 1. Getting started
text: 1. Getting started The desktop app Download the installer for your system from the releases page: System File Windows Marky_…_x64-setup.exe (or the .msi for managed installs) macOS Marky_…_universal.dmg Linux Marky_…_amd64.AppImage or .deb Run it and follow the steps. On Windows, SmartScreen may warn that the installer isn't signed yet: choose More info → Run anyway. Afterwards Markdown files (.md, .markdown) open in Marky when you double-click them, or with Open with → Marky. The desktop app checks for updates (you can switch that off) and installs them only when you agree; see Settings. The web app Open the web app's address in Chrome, Edge, Firefox or Safari. Nothing is installed and nothing about your notes leaves your computer: Marky reads and writes files on your own disk. After the first visit the web app also works offline. Chrome and Edge can open a whole folder and save straight into it. Other browsers open a read-only copy of a folder and download what you save. To give the web app its own window, choose Install Marky in the address bar (Chrome, Edge). On a phone or tablet Open the web app in the browser on your phone or tablet and add it to the home screen: iPhone and iPad (Safari): the share button, then Add to Home Screen. Android (Chrome): the ⋮ menu, then Add to Home screen or Install app. It then opens full screen, like an app, and works offline. On a phone the buttons take two rows. Swipe the lower row (formatting) sideways for more, and tap the command palette button, the last one on the top row, for everything else. The sidebar slides over the text and closes when you pick something. A tablet shows the same layout as a computer. Your first note Start Marky. An empty note, Untitled.md, is open. Type a heading: # Shopping list, press Enter, and a list: - bread. Press Enter again and the next - appears by itself. The preview on the right shows the result as you type. Press Ctrl+S to save. Marky asks where; pick a folder and a name. From now on, Marky keeps a draft of everything you type, even before you save, so nothing is lost if the computer crashes (Your work is safe). Working with a folder Most people keep their notes in a folder (or a few). Open one with Open folder (the second button, or Ctrl+Shift+O). The sidebar lists its notes; click one to open it in a tab. Links between notes, search across all of them, tags and the graph all work on the open folder. Finding any command Everything Marky can do is in the command palette: press F1 (or Ctrl+Shift+P) and type a few letters of what you want, such as export or table. The palette shows the shortcut next to each command, so you learn them as you go.

title: 2. The Marky window
text: 2. The Marky window Part What it's for Toolbar (top) Open, open folder and save; formatting (bold, headings, lists, links, images, tables …); the layout (editor, split, preview); seamless view; the sidebar; theme; plugins; help; settings; the command palette Tabs One per open note. A dot marks unsaved changes; + opens a new note. Middle-click closes a tab Sidebar (left) The open folder's files, search, Git, tags, backlinks, comments, properties and the outline. Show or hide it with Ctrl+Shift+E Editor The Markdown text Preview What the note looks like. It follows the editor as you scroll and type Status bar (bottom) Line and column, words and characters, reading time, the draft state, line endings and encoding; warnings (images without alt text), who's here in a shared note, and the word goal The toolbar From left to right: Open file, Open folder, Save; then the formatting buttons: bold, italic, strikethrough, code, headings 1–3, bulleted, numbered and task lists, quote, link, image, table, code block and horizontal line. Pointing at a button shows its name and shortcut. On the right: the three layouts (Editor only, Split view, Preview only), Seamless view, the sidebar, the theme (light, dark, sepia, high contrast or the system's choice), Plugins, Help, Settings and the command palette. The sidebar The sidebar's panels appear when they have something to show: Files: the open folder as a tree. Click to open; ✎ renames, × deletes (also F2 and Del). The graph button shows how notes link. Search: Ctrl+Shift+F searches all notes in the folder. Git (desktop): changed files, commit and sync. Tags and Backlinks: see Linked notes. Comments: see Reviewing. Properties: the note's front matter as fields. Outline: the note's headings. Click one to go there. On a narrow window the sidebar slides over the editor and closes again once you pick something. The status bar Click the parts that do something: the alt-text warning jumps to the first image without a description, Suggesting switches Suggest mode off, ● Live shows who's in a shared note, and the word goal shows your progress. The command palette F1 or Ctrl+Shift+P opens the palette: every command, searchable. Type a few letters (they don't have to be next to each other: exwo finds Export as Word), use ↑ ↓ and press Enter. Ctrl+P is the file palette: find any note in the folder by name (Desktop: also recently opened files elsewhere). Themes and language The theme button switches between light, dark, sepia, high contrast (WCAG AAA) and system (follows your computer). Marky speaks English and Dutch; it follows your computer's language, or pick one in Settings › Appearance.

title: 3. Writing
text: 3. Writing Markdown in a nutshell Markdown is plain text with a few symbols for formatting. Marky follows GitHub's flavour (CommonMark with tables, task lists, strikethrough and footnotes). Write Get # Title, ## Section … ###### Headings (they also make the Outline) **bold**, _italic_, ~~strike~~, `code` bold, italic, strike, code - item, 1. item, - [ ] task Lists and checklists > quote A quote > [!NOTE] (TIP, IMPORTANT, WARNING, CAUTION) A coloured callout [text](https://…) A link ![description](picture.png) A picture ```js … ``` Code with colours $x^2$, $$ … $$ Math Text[^1] and [^1]: the note A footnote --- (alone, between blank lines) A horizontal line, and a new slide when presenting Enter continues a list (and a numbered list counts on); Enter on an empty item ends the list. Tab and Shift+Tab indent and outdent list items. Formatting shortcuts Action Keys Bold, italic, inline code Ctrl+B, Ctrl+I, Ctrl+E Strikethrough Ctrl+Shift+X Heading 1–6 Ctrl+Alt+1 … 6 Bulleted, numbered, task list Ctrl+Shift+8, 7, 9 Tick a task Ctrl+Enter Quote Ctrl+Shift+. Link Ctrl+K (or paste an address over selected text) Code block Ctrl+Alt+C Shortcuts toggle: Ctrl+B on bold text makes it plain again. The / menu Type / at the start of a line (or after a space) for a menu of things to insert: headings, lists, a table, callouts, a code block, Mermaid and other diagrams, math, a divider, an image, a link, today's date, contents, and your templates. Keep typing to narrow it down (/tab → Table) and press Enter. Tab jumps between the parts to fill in. Templates New note from template… makes a note from a template; Insert template… puts one at the cursor. Built in are meeting notes, decision record, project brief and daily note; the app design kit (app spec, user story, screen with mockup, data model, API endpoint, see AI agents); and, with Architecture work on, concept templates (security, operations, integration, data migration, test). Your own templates are Markdown files in a folder called templates in the open folder. They can use: Placeholder Becomes {{date}}, {{time}}, {{weekday}} Today's date, the time, the day of the week {{title}} The note's name {{cursor}} Where you start typing Properties Front matter is a block of YAML at the very top of a note, between two --- lines. Marky shows it as Properties in the sidebar, where you can edit it without touching YAML: Text and numbers in fields, yes/no as a checkbox, lists such as tags as chips (type and press Enter to add, × to remove). Click a property's name to rename it; the row at the bottom adds one. Comments and formatting in the YAML are kept, and every change can be undone with Ctrl+Z. Some properties mean something to Marky: title (exports and websites), tags, word-goal, bibliography and citation-style (Citations), publish: false and draft: true (publishing a website). Pasting Pictures: paste a screenshot or drop an image file. In a folder, it's saved in assets/ next to the note and linked. Large pictures are made smaller (WebP, at most 1920 px wide; Settings › Editor). From web pages, Word and Google Docs: formatted text becomes clean Markdown (headings, bold, links, lists, tables, code). Ctrl+Shift+V pastes plain text. An address over selected text makes a link. Checks while you type Marky underlines common problems: a skipped heading level, an empty heading, spaces at the end of a line, a link without text, a code block that isn't closed, and (with a folder open) links to notes or files that don't exist. Point at the underline for an explanation and, where the fix is clear, a Fix button. Check links in folder… lists every broken link in the folder. The status bar also warns about pictures without a description (alt text), which screen-reader users need. Spelling With Spellcheck on (Settings › Editor), words Marky doesn't know get a red wavy line. Click one, or put the cursor in it and press Ctrl+., for suggestions, Add to dictionary (your own words, kept on this computer) or Ignore (unti

title: 4. Editing views and focus
text: 4. Editing views and focus Three layouts The three buttons on the right of the toolbar choose what you see: Layout Shortcut Use it for Editor only (the button) Writing without distraction Split view Ctrl+\ Writing with the result next to it (the editor and preview scroll together) Preview only Reading Drag the line between editor and preview to change their sizes. Double-click something in the preview to jump to its line in the text. Three editing views However you edit, the file stays plain Markdown. Pick the view in Settings › Editor › Editing view, or switch with the shortcuts: Markdown source: the text exactly as typed, with colours for the Markdown symbols. Live preview (Ctrl+Alt+L): the symbols are hidden except on the line you're editing. Headings show without #, bold without **, links as their text, bullets as • and task boxes you can click. Seamless (Ctrl+Alt+M, or the page button): like a word processor. On top of live preview, pictures show as pictures, tables as tables, formulas and diagrams drawn, code in a quiet frame, and the properties folded to one line. Click anything, or move the cursor into it, and its Markdown comes back to edit. With the Editor only layout, seamless view is a single document-like page. Focus mode Focus mode (F8) hides everything but the text, centred. Dim other paragraphs fades all but the one you're writing; Typewriter scrolling keeps the line you're writing in the middle of the screen (both in Settings › Editor). Esc or the Exit focus button leaves. Keybindings Settings › Editor › Keybindings: Standard, Vim (normal, insert and visual mode, :w saves) or Emacs (C-x C-s saves, C-a / C-e, C-k …).

title: 5. Files and folders
text: 5. Files and folders Notes and tabs Action Keys New note Alt+N Open a file Ctrl+O, or drag a .md file onto the window Open a folder Ctrl+Shift+O Go to a note in the folder Ctrl+P Save, Save as, Save all Ctrl+S, Ctrl+Shift+S, Ctrl+Alt+S Close the tab; next and previous tab Alt+W; Alt+PgDn, Alt+PgUp Each tab keeps its own undo history, cursor and scroll position. Closing a tab with unsaved changes asks Save, Don't save or Cancel. Line endings (LF or CRLF) and a UTF-8 byte-order mark are kept as they were; the status bar shows them. A file in another encoding (UTF-16, Windows-1252) opens read-only so saving can't damage it; Save as makes a UTF-8 copy. The open folder The sidebar shows the folder's Markdown notes as a tree. Pictures in the folder load in the preview; links to other notes open them in a tab. New note: the + button in the Files panel, or New file in folder…. Rename: ✎ or F2. An open note's tab follows, unsaved changes included; links to it can be updated, and its comments come along. Delete: × or Del. Marky asks first. Desktop: the note goes to the Recycle Bin. Web: browsers have no Recycle Bin, so it's deleted for good. Changes by other programs: a note that changes on disk reloads by itself when you haven't edited it. If you have, a banner offers Compare, Keep my version or Reload from disk. Web: Chrome and Edge can save into the folder you open; other browsers open a read-only copy. Search in the folder Ctrl+Shift+F searches every note in the folder, including unsaved changes in open tabs. The buttons next to the box switch on match case (Aa), whole word (ab) and regular expressions (.*). Click a result to open the note at the match. Replace all asks first; open notes get one change you can undo. Contents that keep themselves up to date Type /contents (or Insert contents) for a list of the headings below it. Saving keeps it up to date. It sits between <!-- toc --> and <!-- tocstop -->, the markers other tools use too. <!-- toc max=4 --> includes deeper headings; a heading ending in <!-- omit in toc --> is left out. Git (desktop) In a Git repository, the Git panel shows changed notes (with a letter in the file tree: M changed, A added, U new), lets you write a message and Commit all, and Pull and Push (when the branch has a remote). The panel shows the branch. Sync conflict copies OneDrive, Dropbox, iCloud and Syncthing sometimes keep two versions of a note (Plan (conflicted copy …).md, Plan-LAPTOP.md). Sync conflict copies… lists them and compares each with the note: take changes over with the arrows, save the note, then remove the copy. Importing a Word document Import Word document (.docx)… turns a Word file into a note: headings, bold, italic, strikethrough, links, bulleted and numbered lists (nested), tables, footnotes and pictures; Word's tracked changes become suggestions in the reviewer's name (Reviewing); Word's comments become comment threads on the same text, with their replies and whether they were resolved. With a folder open, the note is saved in the folder (pictures in assets/, comments beside it). Without one, it opens as a new note with the comments written into the text as ``. Encrypted notes Notes ending in .md.age are encrypted and open with a passphrase. See Your work is safe.

title: 6. Tables
text: 6. Tables Writing a table | Name | Role | Since | |-------|-----------|------:| | Anna | Editor | 2021 | | Ben | Reviewer | 2023 | The second line separates the header from the rows; a : on the right aligns a column right (:--- left, :---: centred). Insert table (toolbar or /table) starts one for you. Typing in a table While the cursor is in a table: Keys What happens Tab / Shift+Tab Next / previous cell (Tab in the last cell adds a row) Enter The cell below (a new row at the bottom) Alt+↑ / Alt+↓ Move the row up / down Alt+← / Alt+→ Move the column left / right Ctrl+Alt+F Line up the columns A table bar appears above the table: add or remove rows and columns, align a column, sort by a column, and Edit table…. The visual table editor Edit table… (or double-click the table in the preview) opens a grid you edit like a spreadsheet: click a cell and type, use the arrow keys, add and delete rows and columns, set alignment, sort. Paste cells straight from Excel or Google Sheets. Done writes the table back as Markdown. From a spreadsheet or CSV Copy cells in Excel or Google Sheets and paste them into the visual table editor. The CSV tables plugin (Plugins) draws ```csv blocks as tables.

title: 7. Pictures, video and diagrams
text: 7. Pictures, video and diagrams Pictures ![A description](picture.png) shows a picture. The description (alt text) is read to screen-reader users and shown if the picture can't load. Paste or drop a picture into the editor. In a folder it's saved in assets/ next to the note; otherwise it's put in the note itself (up to 2 MB). Desktop: a saved note outside a folder also gets an assets/ folder next to it. Size: ![Map](map.png){width=50%} (of the page width) or {width=320} (pixels), or Image size… with the cursor on a picture. Make smaller: Optimize image… saves a smaller WebP copy and updates the link. Pictures from the internet load by default. Switch off Settings › Preview › Load images from the internet so a note can't track you through them. Videos and sound Put a YouTube or Vimeo link in a picture, or on a line of its own: ![Our product demo](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=…) https://vimeo.com/76979871 The preview shows a ▶ play box. Nothing is loaded from YouTube or Vimeo until you click it; then the video plays from youtube-nocookie.com or player.vimeo.com, which don't set tracking cookies before you play. A start time in the link (&t=42s) is kept. Video and sound files get a player: ![Clip](media/clip.mp4), .webm, .mov, .mp3, .m4a, .wav, .ogg, .flac. Exports (PDF, Word) and other Markdown apps see a link to the video. Diagrams A code block with the right language is drawn as a diagram. All of these except PlantUML are drawn on your own computer, follow the light or dark theme, and go into HTML, PDF, Word and PowerPoint as pictures. Mermaid, Graphviz, charts, drawings and math can be switched off in Manage plugins…. Mermaid ```mermaid flowchart LR Idea --> Draft --> Review --> Published ``` Flowcharts, sequence, class, state and entity-relationship diagrams, Gantt charts, pie charts, mind maps, timelines and C4. See mermaid.js.org. Editing a flowchart in the picture: point at a flowchart in the preview and click Edit. Click a box to select it; the bar above the diagram then renames it, adds a box connected to it (Add box), draws an arrow to another box (Connect to…, then click that box) or deletes it with its arrows. Each step changes the diagram's text in the note, so Ctrl+Z undoes it, and the rest of what you wrote (comments, styling, other lines) stays as it was. Done ends editing. Graphviz ```dot digraph { rankdir=LR Idea -> Draft -> "Published" Draft -> Idea [label="rework"] } ``` The DOT language of Graphviz: good for dependency graphs and state machines. A mistake shows Graphviz's message instead of the graph. Charts (Vega-Lite) ```vega-lite { "data": {"values": [{"q": "Q1", "n": 3}, {"q": "Q2", "n": 7}, {"q": "Q3", "n": 5}]}, "mark": "bar", "encoding": { "x": {"field": "q", "type": "nominal", "title": "Quarter"}, "y": {"field": "n", "type": "quantitative", "title": "Customers"} } } ``` Bars, lines, areas, points, pie charts and more: see the Vega-Lite examples. The data can also come from a file in the folder: "data": {"url": "sales.csv"} (CSV, TSV or JSON), so a chart updates when the file does. Addresses on the internet are refused, so opening a note never tells a server about it. Drawings (Excalidraw) Insert or edit a drawing… opens a full-window drawing board (Excalidraw): shapes, arrows, text and freehand drawing with a hand-drawn look. Save drawing (or Ctrl+S) puts it into the note as an ```excalidraw block. With the cursor in that block, the same command opens it again. A drawing kept in its own .excalidraw file (from excalidraw.com, Obsidian or another app) shows with ![Sketch](sketch.excalidraw). Text in drawings uses your system's font in the preview, not Excalidraw's hand-writing font. C4 models (Structurizr) and PlantUML ```structurizr blocks (the Structurizr DSL) are drawn as C4 diagrams on your computer; choose the view with ```structurizr view=Containers. See Architecture documentation. ```plantuml blocks are drawn by a PlantUML server you choose in Settings › Preview (the public one, Kroki, or one

title: 8. Linked notes, tags and the graph
text: 8. Linked notes, tags and the graph Links between notes Two ways to link to another note in the folder: [the plan](projects/plan.md): an ordinary Markdown link, which works everywhere (GitHub, other editors, websites). [[plan]], [[plan#Budget]] or [[plan|our plan]]: a wikilink, by name, to a heading, or with your own text. Typing [[ suggests notes. Click a link in the preview to open the note. A wikilink to a note that doesn't exist yet is shown dimmed; clicking it creates the note. Backlinks The Backlinks panel lists the notes that link to the one you're reading, with the sentence around each link. Click one to go there. Tags Write #tag in the text (or tags: [a, b] in the properties). The Tags panel lists every tag in the folder with how often it's used; click one to search for it. The rename button next to a tag in the panel changes it in every note (renaming to an existing tag merges the two). The graph Show graph of notes (Ctrl+Shift+G, or the graph button in the Files panel) draws your notes as dots and their links as lines. Drag to move around, scroll to zoom, click a note to open it. Notes that nothing links to stand out, so you can find loose ends. The graph beside the editor Like in Obsidian, the graph can stay open next to your note: Ctrl+Alt+G (Graph beside the editor on/off, or Show beside the editor in the large graph). The pane shows the note you're in with its neighbours (Steps sets how far: 1–3 links), and follows you: open another note and the graph centres on that one. Click a dot to open its note; the pane stays, so you can walk through your notes from link to link. Search to make notes stand out, ⤢ for the large graph with all its options, × to close. Marky remembers whether it's open. Architecture documentation Marky has extra help for documenting software architecture with arc42, decision records (ADRs) and concepts (Settings › Features › Architecture work): templates for each, a check that every arc42 chapter is filled in and every decision has a status, a list of decisions, and C4 diagrams from Structurizr models drawn in the preview. Type arc42, ADR or architecture in the command palette to find the commands.

title: 9. Citations
text: 9. Citations Marky cites from a bibliography the way Pandoc and most academic Markdown tools do, so your notes stay compatible. 1. A bibliography Put your references in a file next to the note: BibTeX (.bib): exported by Zotero, JabRef, Mendeley, Google Scholar and most reference managers. CSL-JSON (.json): exported by Zotero (Better CSL JSON) and others. @article{smith2020, author = {Smith, John and Lee, Kim}, title = {Fast Markdown Parsing}, journal = {Communications of the ACM}, year = {2020}, volume = {63}, number = {4}, pages = {12--19}, doi = {10.1145/1234} } 2. Name it in the note --- bibliography: references.bib --- 3. Cite Write Author-date (default) Numbered [@smith2020] (Smith & Lee, 2020) [1] [@smith2020, p. 14] (Smith & Lee, 2020, p. 14) [1, p. 14] [@smith2020; @knuth1984] (Smith & Lee, 2020; Knuth, 1984) [1, 2] [see @knuth1984] (see Knuth, 1984) [see 2] [-@smith2020] (2020) [1] @knuth1984 says Knuth (1984) says Knuth [2] says Three or more authors become García et al. A list of References goes at the end of the note, or where it has a line <!-- references -->. Options Property Does citation-style: numeric Numbers in order of first citation, and a numbered list (also ieee or vancouver) reference-section-title: Literatuur The heading above the list Where citations appear In the preview, the seamless view, and in Word, PDF and HTML exports and published websites. The note itself keeps the [@key] text, so you can still change the style or use Pandoc. A key that isn't in the bibliography stays as [@key], so you can spot typos.

title: 10. Reviewing: suggestions and comments
text: 10. Reviewing: suggestions and comments Two ways to work on a note with others without changing it behind their back: suggest changes they accept or reject, and discuss it in comments. Both work in ordinary notes, in shared notes (Editing together) and in Word round trips. Suggesting changes (track changes) Press Ctrl+Alt+T (or Suggest changes (track changes) on/off). The first time Marky asks your name. While Suggest mode is on, the status bar says Suggesting, and: what you type shows green and underlined; what you delete shows red and struck through; hovering shows who suggested it and when. Accept or reject a suggestion with its ✓ and ✗. The bar above the editor counts the suggestions, moves between them (‹ ›) and has Accept all and Reject all. Ctrl+Z undoes any of it. In the file, suggestions are CriticMarkup, plain text that survives Git and other editors: We use PostgreSQL for all services. added, , `new`, and for who and when. `` shows as 💬, text as a highlight. When you export a note with suggestions, Marky asks whether to show them, or take them all accepted or all rejected. Word gets real tracked changes. Comments Select text and press Ctrl+Alt+N (with nothing selected, the word at the cursor is used). Type your comment in the Comments panel and press Ctrl+Enter. The commented text gets a light yellow highlight; click it, or the quote in the panel, to open its thread. Reply, Resolve (it's hidden under Show resolved threads), Reopen or Delete. Your own replies have a ×. Comments are kept in a file beside the note, note.md.comments.json (or all together in .marky/comments, Settings › General). The note stays clean Markdown. When the note changes elsewhere, each comment finds its text again from the words around it. If its text was deleted, the thread moves to Detached instead of disappearing. Comments need a note in an open folder. @mentions Type @ in a comment or reply and pick someone from the list: the people who commented or suggested in the note, and who's in a shared note with you. ↑ ↓ choose, Enter or Tab picks, Esc closes the list. Mentions are coloured; a mention of you stands out and its thread gets a blue edge on the left. Mentioning me (N) above the threads shows only the threads that mention you. In a shared note, a new comment that mentions you pops up a notice. @Claude asks the AI agent (desktop): the thread shows Waiting for Claude until it answers. See chapter 14. Round trips with Word Export: Export as Word (.docx) asks whether to include open comments; they become Word comments on the same text, replies as a thread. Suggestions become tracked changes. Import: Import Word document (.docx)… turns Word's tracked changes into suggestions and its comments into threads, with replies and resolved state. So a reviewer who only uses Word can comment and track changes there, and you bring their work back into Marky.

title: 11. Editing together, live
text: 11. Editing together, live Several people can edit one note at the same time, each in Marky in their browser or the desktop app, and see each other's cursors. What you need A live-editing server: a small Marky relay that your organisation runs (a Docker image; see the relay documentation). It only passes on encrypted messages and can't read the notes. When you use the Marky web app that the relay itself serves, Marky finds it by itself. Sharing a note Open the note and run Share for live editing…. The first time, fill in the server's address; it's remembered (Settings › General). Start sharing. Marky asks your name once, so the others see who's who. Pick your colour in Settings › General. You get three links: Link Whoever has it can … Edit link change the note Review link suggest changes and comment, but not change the text directly Read-only link read along Copy one and send it. The link is the key: share it only with the people it's for. Joining Opening a link starts Marky with the shared note in a tab of its own (Desktop: Join a shared note… and paste the link). The keys disappear from the address bar once you're in. While you edit together You see the others' cursors with their names; the status bar shows ● Live and who's here. Click it for the links and the people. Ctrl+Z undoes only your own changes. Comments are shared too: new threads and replies appear for everyone at once, on the right words. Suggestions work as usual. Offline: if the connection drops, the status bar says Live · reconnecting…; keep typing and everything merges when it's back. Reviewers Someone who opens a review link is always in Suggest mode: the status bar says Reviewing, everything they type or delete becomes a suggestion in their name, and they can't accept or reject suggestions; the editors decide. Reviewers can pass on review and read-only links, not edit links. A review link contains the edit key, and Marky (not the encryption) keeps reviewers to suggestions. Give review links to people you'd trust with an edit link. Who wrote what Show who wrote what (shared notes) on/off gives each person's text a light background in their colour, with a legend above the note and their name when you point at a passage. Text from before sharing belongs to whoever shared the note. The version history of a shared note also says who changed each version (Your work is safe). Your file For the person who shared it, the note stays an ordinary file, saved as always. Close it (or Marky) while the others keep editing, and reopening it reconnects and brings in what changed meanwhile. If the file changes outside Marky (a Git pull), the change is merged in for everyone. Stopping Stop sharing here (or Leave) disconnects you; the others carry on. End sharing for everyone disconnects everyone and makes all links stop working. Everybody keeps the text they have. Privacy and limits Everything is encrypted on your computer before it leaves, with a key that's only in the link. The server can't read the note, the names or the comments; changes are signed, so read-only links can't change anything. The server keeps the encrypted note for those who join later, until sharing ends or nobody has changed it for 30 days. Names aren't checked: there are no accounts. Trust a name as much as you trust the people you sent the link to. Notes up to 8 MB can be shared. Encrypted notes can't be shared live.

title: 12. Your work is safe
text: 12. Your work is safe Drafts and recovery Every open note is saved as a draft in the background within a few seconds of typing, separately from your file. The status bar says Draft saved. After a crash, a power cut or an accidental reload, Marky lists the notes with unsaved work and offers to restore them. Your open tabs and folder come back the next time you start. Desktop: saving is atomic: the new version is written to a temporary file first and then put in place, so a crash never leaves a half-written file. Version history Every time you save, Marky keeps a copy (the last 100 per note, and the note as it was before Marky first changed it). Version history… lists them: Each version shows when it was saved, how long it was, and by whom: you, or in a shared note the people who typed since the version before. Pick one to compare it side by side with the note now. Restore this version puts it back as one change you can undo. The copies are kept on this computer only. Forget this file's history removes them. Encrypted notes Keep a note readable only with a passphrase: passwords, personal matters, anything confidential. Encrypting a note Open the note (saved, in a folder) and run Encrypt this note (passphrase)…. Choose a passphrase of at least 10 characters. A few words works well: correct horse battery staple. Marky refuses passphrases that are easy to guess. Type it again. Confirm. The note is saved as note.md.age, and the unencrypted note.md is removed, together with its version history, draft and comments. Opening an encrypted note Encrypted notes have a 🔒 in the folder and on their tab. Clicking one asks for the passphrase; a wrong one asks again. Edit and save as usual: every save is encrypted again with the same passphrase. What Marky never does with an encrypted note No drafts and no version history (they'd be stored unencrypted). Not in search, the index, tags, backlinks or the graph. No comments (use a `` in the text instead). Not sent to AI agents, not readable by plugins, not shared live. Not reopened when Marky restarts: open it again with its passphrase. Taking the encryption off Remove encryption from this note… saves it as an ordinary note.md again. The format age, with scrypt to turn the passphrase into a key and ChaCha20-Poly1305 to encrypt, written as text so it works in Git. The age command-line tool opens the same files: age -d note.md.age > note.md. Nobody can open the note without the passphrase: not Marky, not its makers, not you. Keep it somewhere safe, like a password manager.

title: 13. Export, publish and present
text: 13. Export, publish and present All exports are in the command palette (type export). When a note has suggestions, Marky first asks whether to show them, or take them accepted or rejected. Export What you get HTML One self-contained file, pictures and diagrams included; a mockup shows as the page itself PDF (Ctrl+Alt+P) The print dialog with print styling; choose Save as PDF PDF with options A cover page, contents, header and footer, page numbers and a style Word (.docx) Real Word headings, lists, tables, footnotes, pictures and diagrams; tracked changes and comments PowerPoint (.pptx) Your slides, editable in PowerPoint Website A folder of notes as a website Copy as rich text For e-mail, Google Docs or Word Copy for Confluence, Slack or plain text In their own formatting Confluence (desktop) The note as a Confluence page Pandoc (desktop) EPUB, LaTeX or OpenDocument, if Pandoc is installed PDF with options Export as PDF with options…: a cover page with title, subtitle, author, date and a logo; a table of contents; header and footer text ({title}, {date} fill themselves in) and page numbers; a style: standard, serif, compact or minimal, plus your own CSS file; save it all as a preset; Report and Academic are built in. Word Headings become Word's heading styles, so Word's navigation and table of contents work. Code is set in Consolas, math as TeX text, diagrams and mockups as pictures, citations as text with the list of references. With a Word template (Word template for exports…: your organisation's .docx or .dotx), exports get its headers, footers, logo, fonts and styles. Put {{content}} in the template where the text belongs; {{title}}, {{author}} and {{date}} are filled in. Slides Every --- on a line of its own (between blank lines) starts a new slide, as in Marp. Present (F5): ← → or click to move, F for full screen, Esc to leave. It starts at the slide your cursor is in. A slide with just a heading is centred like a title page; long slides shrink their text to fit. Export slides as PDF: one slide per 16:9 page. Export slides as PowerPoint (.pptx): a file you can keep editing in PowerPoint, Keynote or Google Slides. The first heading becomes the slide's title, lists become bullets (with their levels), code a box in Consolas, tables real tables, pictures and diagrams pictures. Publishing a folder as a website Publish folder as a website… turns the open folder into a website: every note becomes a page. This manual is made that way. Pages: guide/intro.md becomes guide/intro.html, with the folder as navigation on the left, the page's contents on the right, search at the top and previous / next at the bottom. Light or dark, following the reader's system; on a phone the navigation folds into a ☰ menu. The front page is index.md or README.md; without one, Marky makes a list of all pages. A page's title is title: from its properties, else its first heading. Everything works: links between notes (also [[wikilinks]]) point at the pages, pictures and media files are copied, diagrams are drawn, citations filled in. Suggestions show accepted, comments are left out. Left out: notes with publish: false or draft: true, encrypted notes, and folders whose name starts with _. Where it goes: Save as .zip, or Write to _site in the folder. Put the files on any web server, or on GitHub Pages: push the contents of _site to a gh-pages branch (or a docs/ folder) and switch on Pages in the repository's settings. Marky adds the .nojekyll file GitHub needs. Publishing one note as a page Publish note as a page (link)… gives one note a link that anyone can open in a browser to read it, drawn as in the preview, without Marky or an account. Use it for a plan you want feedback on, a status page, or a spec for people outside your team. What readers see: the note as a clean page: diagrams, charts, math, mockups and pictures included, suggestions accepted and comments left out. A Dark button and Print are at the top. Links to your other notes don't lead anywhe

title: 14. AI agents (desktop)
text: 14. AI agents (desktop) Marky works with the AI coding agents you may already use: Claude Code, OpenAI Codex and Gemini CLI. They run on your computer with your own account; Marky gives them tools to read and search your notes and to propose changes, which you accept or reject. Starting an agent Start Claude Code in the terminal (or Start Codex / Start Gemini CLI) opens Marky's terminal (Ctrl+`) with the agent already connected to Marky. Ask it about your notes: summarise what we decided about the database, find notes that contradict each other, write release notes from these changes. What agents can do Read and search the open folder's notes (not encrypted ones), the open tab, and text in pictures (when OCR is on). Propose changes: a proposal shows as an inline difference in the note. Accept, Reject, or Keep as suggestions (the agent's changes become suggestions in its name, to review later or hand to someone else). Create notes: you see the new note as a proposal; when you accept it, it's written to the folder and opened. Change several notes at once: renaming a term everywhere, or bringing specs in line with a changed story, comes as one change set (see below). Read and answer comments: write @Claude in a comment and the agent sees it waiting for it. It makes the change you asked for (as a proposal), replies in the thread and resolves it. Its comments are marked AI. Agents can't save, change or delete your notes themselves: a change waits for you, and only a new note you accept is written at once. The one thing they write without asking is comments: only in the note's comments file, never in its text, with a notice each time. Reviewing an agent's work Review a plan or spec an agent wrote the way you'd review a colleague's: select text, add a comment (Ctrl+Alt+N) and mention @Claude (it's in the list when you type @). The thread shows Waiting for Claude. Then tell Claude Code handle my comments in Marky: it finds every thread that asks it something, in any note of the folder, proposes the changes, answers each thread and resolves it. Reply with another @Claude to go on; a thread without a mention is left to people. Changes across several notes When an agent's change touches more than one note, it arrives as one change set: a dialog lists every note it changes (new for notes it creates), with the lines added and removed, and shows each note's change when you click it. Untick the notes you don't want, then Apply. Everything you kept is applied together: open notes get the change in the editor (Ctrl+Z works, you save as usual), closed notes are written. Undo in the bar that follows puts all of them back, except a note someone changed since, which is left as it is. Keep as suggestions puts the changes into the notes as suggestions in the agent's name; Later puts the review aside (a bar above the editor brings it back); Reject all changes nothing. Marky checks every edit before showing anything: if one of them doesn't fit its note, the whole set is refused and the agent is told which one. Notes that may be out of date A spec written from a story, or a screen built on an ADR, can say so in its properties: based_on: - ../stories/checkout.md - "[[Payment ADR]]" Mark note as up to date with its sources (command palette) records a fingerprint of each source next to it (checkout.md@3f9a2c1b), and Marky keeps a copy of the source as it was. Sources can also be code in the folder (- ../src/checkout/pay.ts): a spec that lists the code it describes is flagged when that code changes. When a source's text changes later (a note's properties don't count), the note shows a bar: This note may be out of date. Show what changed shows the source's changes since the check; Mark as up to date records that the note is in line again. Notes that may be out of date… lists every such note in the folder, including sources that are missing or were never checked. Agents can do the checking for you: tell Claude Code bring the specs in line with the stories. I

title: 15. Settings and plugins
text: 15. Settings and plugins Settings Open them with Ctrl+, or the gear button. Changes apply at once. Section Settings General Your name (with your suggestions and comments, and in shared notes); your colour when editing together; where comments are kept; the live-editing server. Desktop: check for updates; the Confluence address, e-mail and space Appearance Theme (system, light, dark, sepia, high contrast); language (English, Nederlands) Editor Font and size, readable line length, word wrap, line numbers, spellcheck, Markdown checks, the editing view, keybindings (Standard, Vim, Emacs), focus-mode options, how pasted pictures are stored. Desktop: titles for pasted web addresses Preview Font size, scroll sync, the PlantUML server, loading pictures from the internet, your own CSS for the preview and exports Features Switch off what you don't use (Git and AI on the desktop; tags and backlinks, the graph, slides, contents blocks, architecture work, sync-conflict notices). Nothing is deleted. Desktop: which AI agent the writing assistant uses Export and Import save your settings to a file and read them back (handy on a second computer); Reset restores the defaults. Updates (desktop) Marky checks for a new version when it starts (switch this off in Settings › General) and asks before installing. Check for updates in the palette checks now. Updates are signed: Marky only installs a version signed by its makers. Plugins Manage plugins… (the plug button) lists the plugins. Built in (switch them off if you don't need them): Math, Diagrams (Mermaid), Graphs (Graphviz), Charts (Vega-Lite), Drawings (Excalidraw). The plugin market Plugin market › Browse shows plugins you can add: Kanban boards, CSV tables, calculations, QR codes, readability, repeated words, change case, a focus timer and more. Search, or pick a category. Details shows what a plugin does, what it's allowed to do, in plain words, and what changed in the latest version. Before installing, Marky shows the permissions again and asks. Installed plugins with a newer version show Update to …; if an update asks for more than before, the new permissions are marked. Marky fetches the list only when you click Browse, only shows a list signed by Marky's maintainer, and checks every plugin it downloads against that list. How plugins are kept safe Plugins run in a sandbox without network access, and only get what they asked for and you allowed (read the note, change it, add commands, draw code blocks …). A plugin that crashes or hangs is switched off. If something misbehaves, Restart in safe mode starts Marky without plugins. Plugins can't read encrypted notes. You can also install a plugin from a .js file, and write your own: see the plugin documentation in the Marky repository. The command line marky-cli.mjs (on the releases page, needs Node.js 20 or later) runs Marky's checks and exports in a terminal or a CI pipeline: node marky-cli.mjs lint docs/ # check every note in docs/ node marky-cli.mjs lint docs/ --fix # and fix what's clear node marky-cli.mjs lint docs/ --format github # annotations in GitHub Actions node marky-cli.mjs export note.md --html # or --docx, or --pdf node marky-cli.mjs tokens design.md --format tailwind4 -o src/theme.css tokens writes the design tokens of a note's tokens blocks (or of a tokens .json/.yaml file) as css (the default), scss, json, tailwind4, tailwind3 or ts, to the screen or to -o. lint ends with exit code 1 when it finds problems, so a pipeline can fail on them.

title: 17. Troubleshooting
text: 17. Troubleshooting Problem What to do Windows warns about the installer Expected until the installer is signed: More info → Run anyway Desktop: "Access denied: Marky can only use files and folders you opened" Marky only touches files you opened yourself, as a protection against harmful documents. Open the file or its folder again (Ctrl+O, Ctrl+Shift+O) Web: I can't save into the folder Only Chrome and Edge can write to a folder; other browsers open a read-only copy and download what you save Pictures from the web don't show Settings › Preview › Load images from the internet has been switched off (it's on by default); switch it on to show them A very large note (several MB) feels slower The preview waits until you pause typing; everything else stays quick. Notes up to 10 MB are supported Something odd after installing a plugin Restart in safe mode, then remove the plugin in Manage plugins… The plugin market says the list isn't signed The list was changed on the way. Nothing is shown or installed; try later A comment is under Detached The text it was on was changed or deleted. Read it, then resolve or delete it "That shared note isn't available any more" Sharing was ended, or nobody changed it for 30 days. Ask for a new link Live · reconnecting… The connection dropped. Keep typing; Marky reconnects and everything merges "This browser can't do the encryption live editing needs" Use a recent Chrome, Edge, Firefox or Safari 17+, or the desktop app "That passphrase doesn't open …" Passphrases are case-sensitive; check Caps Lock. Without the right passphrase nobody can open the note A chart "only reads data from the open folder" Charts don't load data from the internet. Put the data file in the folder and use its name: "url": "data.csv" Citations show as [@key] The note needs bibliography: file.bib in its properties, the file must be in the folder, and the key must be in it A video is only a link in an export Exports can't play videos, so they link to them Desktop: "Codex isn't installed" / "Gemini CLI isn't installed" Install it and sign in once in a terminal, or pick another agent in Settings › Features Reporting a bug About Marky → Copy diagnostic report (versions and settings, never your notes) and include it

title: Marky Manual
text: Marky Manual Marky is a Markdown editor with a live preview, for notes, documentation, reports and everything in between. It runs in your browser (the web app) and as a program for Windows, macOS and Linux (the desktop app). Both look and work the same; where they differ, this manual says Desktop or Web. This manual walks through everything Marky does, with a picture of each part. Read it front to back to learn Marky, or jump to the chapter you need. The navigation on the left lists the chapters; the search box at the top searches all of them. The chapters Chapter What's in it 1 Getting started Installing Marky on your computer, using it in a browser or on a phone, and a first note 2 The Marky window The toolbar, tabs, editor, preview, sidebar and status bar, and the command palette 3 Writing Markdown, formatting shortcuts, the / menu, templates, properties, checks and the writing assistant 4 Editing views and focus Source, live preview and seamless view; layouts; focus and typewriter mode 5 Files and folders Tabs, folders, search, renaming, Git, sync copies and importing Word documents 6 Tables Writing tables, the table bar and the visual table editor 7 Pictures, video and diagrams Images, click-to-load videos, Mermaid, Graphviz, charts, drawings, C4 and PlantUML 8 Linked notes, tags and the graph Wikilinks, backlinks, tags and the graph of your notes 9 Citations Citing from a BibTeX or CSL-JSON bibliography 10 Reviewing: suggestions and comments Track changes, comments, @mentions and Word round trips 11 Editing together, live Sharing a note, the three kinds of link, who wrote what 12 Your work is safe Drafts, recovery, version history and encrypted notes 13 Export, publish and present HTML, PDF, Word, PowerPoint, slides, websites and Confluence 14 AI agents Claude Code, Codex and Gemini with your notes (desktop) 15 Settings and plugins Every setting, the built-in plugins and the plugin market 16 Keyboard shortcuts All shortcuts on one page 17 Troubleshooting What to do when something doesn't work On a Mac, read Ctrl as ⌘ throughout.
